OC. 282 334 1306, but in compounds ξύγγνοιαν [kinship] Ant. 66. ξυλλάβετον [you two take hold] Ph. 1003. ξύμπας [all together] 1243. ξύμπαντες [all together] OC. 1646. ξύμπλουν [sailing together] Ant. 541. ξύμφημι [I agree] El. 1257. Ai. 278. Ph. 1310. OR. 553 642. ξυνηντίαζον [they were meeting] 804. ξύναιμον [kindred] Ai. 127. Ant. 659. Συνάπτετον [you two join] El. 21. ξυναρπάσειαν [they might seize] Ai. 840. Συναρπάσας [having seized] OC. 819. ξύνειμι [I am with] El. 264 276 161. ξύνεστι [he is with] Tr. 199. ξυνών [being with] El. 1359. ξυνηγορεῖς [you advocate] Tr. 874. Ξυνήδομαι [I rejoice with] OC. 1398. ξυνθήματα [signals] Tr. 158. ξύνοικος [dwelling with] El. 785 818 and in Aeschylus the simple ξύν [with] Pers. 777. Ch. 460 1035. Eum. 457 945 1024, but in compounds Pr. 685. Sept. 188 352 354 510. Pers. 177. Ag. 213 650 1208. Ch. 31 460 599 812 978. Eum. 509 520 531 712. Suppl. 65 467 493. On the other hand σύν [with] Ag. 1221 1549. Ch. 148. Suppl. 22 975 and in compounds σύμφθογγος [sounding together] Ag. 1107 (where Triclinius has ξύμφθογγος) συνεξελαύνει [he drives out together] 1606. σύνοιδα [I know with] Ch. 217 and in Sophocles σύν [with] OC. 1257. OR. 146 σὺν (apogr. ξὺν) τῷ θεῶ [with the god]. and in compounds σύγκαμνε [toil together] El. 987, where some copies have ξύγκαμνε, and σύγγνωτε [you know together] fr. 609 (in Stobaeus 74, 16). In the remaining feet of the trimeter the scribes wrote sometimes σύν, sometimes ξύν. Those who did not wish to imitate their rashness devised various rules by which the use of each form was restricted. Porson judged that σύν was not to be tolerated except where it was required by the metre, while Elmsley (in the Preface to Sophocles' Oedipus Rex p. XII) approved σύν after short vowels, unless they had to be lengthened for the metre, and ξύν after long vowels. Most recently Herwerden in the Preface to Sophocles' Oedipus Rex p. VII, having collected examples of both spellings from the Medicean codex, proposed the following rules, according to which he himself corrected not a few passages of Sophocles and thought that the other tragedians, who likely followed the same rules, should also be corrected: "σύν is placed before a consonant, ξύν before a vowel, equally outside composition and in composition, e.g. συγγνώμη [pardon], σύγγονος [kinsman], συγκαθαρμόζειν [to fit together], συγκαταίθειν [to burn together], but ξυνάδειν [to sing with], ξυναλγεῖν [to grieve with], ξυνάπτειν [to join], ξυναιρεῖν [to take together]. Exception 1. At the beginning of a verse, even before a consonant, the form ξύν is rather used. Exception 2. For euphony, both after the letter ξ and where the following syllable ends in ξ, κ or χ, even before a vowel, the form ξύν is used." Since no probable reason for these rules can be adduced and no indications are found in Aristophanes and the other Attic writers, no one will easily persuade himself that the Attic form ξύν must be expelled from most passages of the tragedians to satisfy those rules. Therefore Porson's opinion seems to me more probable, although it must be circumscribed within somewhat narrower limits. For just as the tragedians in the fifth foot of the trimeter, when the preceding final syllable is short, or is regarded as equivalent to it by a short enclitic word (as γραμμάτων τε συνθέσεις [and compositions of letters] in Aesch. Prom. 460 and ἐνοδίους τε συμβόλους [and wayside tokens] 487. Eum. 291 τε σύμμαχου [and ally]), necessarily had to write σύν, not ξύν, e.g. in Aeschylus Pr. 758 ἰδοῦσα συμφοράν [having seen the misfortune]. Sept. [13 ᾧ ' στι συμπρ συμπρεπές.] 611 ἀνοσίοισι συμμιγείς [mingled with the unholy]. Pers. 291 ἥδε συμφορά [this misfortune]. 793 δὲ συμμαχεῖ [and fights as an ally]. Ag. 8 τὸ σύμβολον [the token]. 585 δὲ συντόμως [and concisely]. 884 ὥστε σύγγονον [so that kindred]. Fr. 171 ἔνθα συμβολάς [where meetings], and in Sophocles OR. 135 κἀμὲ σύμμαχον [and me as an ally]. 710 τῷδε σύντομα [to this concise]. 810 ἀλλὰ συντόμως [but concisely]. 1113 τἀνδρὶ σύμμετρος [commensurate with the man] (where in Lest ξύμμετρος), so as not to violate the law observed by the tragedians in this position of the verse, about which I spoke in the Prolegomena to the Scenic Poets p. 37, so it is likely that after the penthemimeral caesura, where the fifth syllable is short, they preferred to say σύν rather than ξύν, because the latter would lengthen the preceding syllable: although the manuscripts sometimes violate this rule too, as in Sophocles OR. 84 τάχ᾽ εἰσόμεσθα· ξύμμετρος γὰρ ὡς κλύειν [we shall soon know; for he is commensurate to hear]. Ph. 675 νοσοῦν ποθεῖ σε ξυμπαραστάτην λαβεῖν [being sick, it longs to take you as a helper]. and in the words of two persons OC. 46 τί δ᾽ ἐστὶ τοῦτο ; ΟΙ. ξυμφορᾶς Σύνθημ᾽ ἐμῆς [What is this? Oedipus: A token of my misfortune]. and in Aeschylus in two places, Pers. 528 πιστοῖσι πιστὰ ξυμφέρειν βουλεύματα [to bring faithful counsels to the faithful], and Suppl. 342 ἀλλ᾽ ἡ δίκη γε ξυμμάχων ὑπερστατεῖ [but justice stands over allies], where undoubtedly συμφέρει and συμμάχων should be written, as in all other such places σύν, both simple and in compounds, not ξύν, is written: see Pr. 496 971. Pers. 350 445 471 846. Ag. 629 1184. Ch. 19 497 906. Eum. 415 610 694. Suppl. 342 437. But if the tragedians observed this law, it is probable that they preferred to keep the trochaic dipodies ending in a short syllable pure rather than to end them with a spondee by introducing ξύν. About euphony, however, the matter is very uncertain. For although it is not improbable that Sophocles Ph. 122 preferred to write ἅπαξ συνήνεσα [once I agreed] rather than ἅπαξ ξυνήνεσα, and the ancients would not have said ξυγξαίνω ξυγξενιτεύω ξυγξέω ξυγξηραίνω ξυγξυρέω ξυγξύω, if they had used these or similar verbs, yet it does not follow that ξύν was considered alien in places where a harsher letter recurred in the next syllable, as σὺν ἐξόδῳ [with the expedition] in OC. 1288, or two words compounded with this preposition followed one another, as ξυμφορᾶς ξύνθημ᾽ ἐμῆς [a token of my misfortune] in Soph. OC. 46 is written in the codex, unless here συμφορᾶς should be written for the reason just mentioned. Nor do the letters ξ and ζ seem to have prevented the preference for ξύν, as ξύζυγος [yoked together] is read in Aeschylus Ch. 599 and several times in Euripides, (but σύζωματα [girdles] in Aesch. Suppl. 462,) ξαίνειν ξυζωσάμενος [having girded oneself to card] in Arist. Lys. 536, although the same are written elsewhere with σ, as σύζωσον [gird] in Arist. Thesm. 255, to which ξύζωσον should be restored. I wrote these things in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 457 458, now I have proposed them with new additions. On the use of the prepositions μετά and σύν T. Mommsen wrote an excellent dissertation in the Program of the Frankfurt Gymnasium a/M. published in 1874, in which he shows that in the older writers σύν is much more frequent than μετά. In Aeschylus there are eight examples of the preposition μετά constructed with the genitive, σύν sixty-seven, in Sophocles 23 and 91, Euripides 101 and 197, on the other hand in Aristophanes μετά 85 and σύν 22, in Thucydides 400 and 37, Plato 586 and 37, Demosthenes 346 and 12 (15), Aristotle 300 and 8. Xenophon departed from the usage of his age, who used μετά with the genitive in 275 places, but σύν in 556 places.
